readerTitle: Why Amazon drew its business as a circle, not a funnel
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon의 플라이휠) + 일화 (냅킨 스케치) + 가상 사례 (원예 용품점, 사내 데이터팀)
insight: 성장을 '위에서 붓고 아래로 새는 깔때기'가 아니라 '고객 한 명이 다음 고객을 데려오는 고리'로 볼 수 있다. 무엇을 고칠지는 각 판매가 다음 판매로 이어지는지에 달려 있다.
misconception: 고객을 더 얻으려면 깔때기 위쪽에 광고를 더 부어 넣는 수밖에 없다.

sources.text: Amazon, company materials describing its 'flywheel' / virtuous cycle (selection, customer experience, traffic, sellers, lower cost structure, lower prices)
Collins, J. (2019). Turning the Flywheel. HarperCollins.
원예 용품점, 사내 데이터팀 사례와 차트 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Amazon 플라이휠의 구성 요소(가격·선택지·고객 경험·트래픽·판매자·비용 구조)는 Amazon 자료와 Collins(2019)로 게시 전 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적인 표현으로만 적었습니다.
'2001년경 냅킨에 그렸다'는 이야기는 널리 전해지는 일화입니다. 연도와 냅킨 여부는 출처마다 다를 수 있어 카드에 'often told', 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다.

cards.title: Why Amazon drew its business as a circle, not a funnel
body: Most companies picture growth as a funnel. Pour people in at the top, lose most of them on the way down, and a few customers drip out the bottom.
Amazon's leaders drew something else. In a story often told about the early 2000s, they sketched their business as a loop, reportedly on a napkin. That shape changed what they chose to work on.

image.label: A funnel next to a looping circle of arrows
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에는 위에서 작은 사람 모양이 쏟아져 들어가고 아래로 몇 명만 나오는 깔때기. 오른쪽에는 화살표가 원을 그리며 돌고, 원을 돌 때마다 사람 모양이 늘어남. 냅킨 위에 그린 느낌의 배경. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your garden shop has stopped growing.
body: You run a garden supply shop with a small online store. Most new customers come from paid ads. Sales were growing, but they've flattened.
You have budget for one fix this quarter. Which do you choose?

options.text: Raise ad spend by 30% to bring in more shoppers
options.feedback: It will likely add customers, but only as long as you keep paying. Stop the ads and the extra customers stop too.

options.text: Fix the checkout, where many shoppers give up
options.feedback: A solid fix that gets more out of every visitor. But each customer still ends at the bottom of the funnel and brings no one new.

options.text: Get every buyer to post a photo of their finished garden, shown on your site and in local searches
options.feedback: Each sale now creates something that attracts the next shopper. It's slower to start, but it can keep working after you stop paying.

cards.title: Each turn of the circle feeds the next.
body: Amazon's version, which it calls a **flywheel**, goes roughly like this. Wide selection and low prices give customers a good experience. Happy customers bring more traffic. More traffic attracts outside sellers. More sellers add more selection.
Growth also spreads fixed costs over more sales, which helps keep prices low. Then the circle turns again.
The point of the drawing: no single step is the goal. Each one exists to push the next.

cards.title: Funnels vs loops
body: A **funnel** is a straight line. People enter at the top, some drop out at each step, and the process ends with a customer. To get more customers, you pour more in.
A **loop** is a circle. Something each customer produces, like a review, a photo, a recommendation or profit to reinvest, becomes the input that brings in the next customer.
Funnels add. Loops can compound, because yesterday's customers help create today's.

image.label: Funnel ending in one customer vs loop returning to the start
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 'Visit → Browse → Buy'로 끝나는 깔때기, 끝에 'End'. 오른쪽: 'Buy → Post a review → New shopper finds it → Buy'로 다시 처음으로 돌아오는 원. 원 쪽 화살표를 강조 색으로.

cards.title: Same ads, different shape.
body: Both shops get 20 new customers a month from ads. In the second shop, each new customer brings in half a customer the next month, through photos and recommendations.
By month six, the shop with a loop is winning almost **twice as many** new customers for the same ad spend.

cards.title: Loops come in a few common shapes.
body: To find a loop, ask what a customer leaves behind that a future customer could see or use.
list: **Content:** reviews and photos help new shoppers find and trust you
**Word of mouth:** happy customers tell people like them
**Money:** profit from one customer pays to win the next
**Two sides:** more buyers attract more sellers, who attract more buyers
cards.callout: A funnel asks where people drop out. A loop asks what each customer gives back.
cards.softwareNote: In software, a loop can be a shared document or invite that shows the product to someone new. Each user who shares becomes a doorway for the next user.

cards.title: Most loops don't run on their own.
body: In the chart, new customers level off near 40 a month. The loop multiplies the ads but can't replace them, because each customer brings in less than one more. Very few loops ever pass that line.
Loops can also run backward. Bad reviews bring fewer customers, which bring fewer good reviews.
And funnels still matter. A funnel shows where people leak out. Fixing those leaks is often what makes a loop work at all.

cards.title: Now you lead a data team inside a big company.
body: Your team built a sales dashboard. Three departments use it. Leadership wants all twelve using it by year end, and you have no extra headcount.
What's your main move?

options.text: Run a series of company-wide emails and training sessions
options.feedback: It will reach people, but every new user costs your team time. Growth stops the day you stop running sessions.

options.text: Make every chart easy to share in meetings, with a link that lets viewers build their own
options.feedback: Each user's work shows the tool to new colleagues at the moment they need it. Usage grows from use itself, though it needs a good first experience to start.

options.text: Ask an executive to make the dashboard mandatory
options.feedback: You may get logins fast, but forced users rarely share or praise a tool. That can start the loop running backward.

cards.title: Ask whether each customer helps bring the next one.
body: A funnel tells you where people drop out. A loop tells you how today's customers can create tomorrow's. The strongest growth plans use both.
**Try it today:** draw your business as a circle. Write what a customer leaves behind, and an arrow to how it could reach a new customer. Where does the arrow break?
